CHARACTER ECOLOGY — DISCOVERING MORE WAYS TO EXPERIENCE THE WORLD

Irreverents • Proposed character and power content • 22 November 2026

# The approved skeleton

Playable characters belong to recognizable functional types, like LEGO Star Wars: droid, bounty hunter or Force user are major mechanical distinctions, while individual characters may have charming personal variations and unique moves. There is a limited expedition roster selected from an expanding permanent cast, Ultimate Alliance-style. Players may switch between these characters, and online co-op uses ONE SHARED PARTY. New recruitments occur throughout the world, including much later than areas where a recruit's ability would have been useful.

Separate from these inherent traits, heroes can acquire temporary weapons and powers from enemies and world objects, Kirby-style. The exact number of power slots, stacking, transfer, dropping and persistence remains undecided.

# Design objective

A character unlock should change the meaning of familiar environments. A player should immediately remember an earlier locked passage, suspicious creature, high roof or blocked machine and wonder whether this newly recruited character could do something there.

The cast is not primarily a collectible trophy roster. Character identity alters affordances and style. Two characters may satisfy the same major type while feeling different in movement, personality, signature action or aesthetic.

# How to invent characters

Start with a WORLD CAPABILITY, not a hairstyle. What can this type do that the player could not do before?

Then invent an individual special characteristic, not necessarily unique to the entire game.

Then invent an expressive tiny pixel silhouette consistent with the preferred GBA-like style. Avoid anime human proportions and existing Kirby shapes.

Finally place the character in a location where discovering their capability feels like finding a new world, not buying an item from an abstract menu.

All characters below are working concepts, with descriptive placeholders rather than final names.

# Candidate functional types (not an approved final taxonomy)

THE GRAPPLER / STRONG ONE — can seize, carry and throw opponents or large objects; specific member could perform exceptional suplexes, withstand collisions or hold a heavy mechanism. Supports impact-first combat, object-based puzzles and heist escapes.

THE TINY INFILTRATOR — small enough for vents, cracks and narrow tunnels; one member may excel at pickpocketing or hiding, another at silent movement or slipping out of restraints. Supports secret routes and covert access.

THE FLYER / GLIDER — reaches elevations, crosses openings and finds aerial routes; some can sustain flight, others ride wind or drop powerful dive attacks.

THE CREATURE-SPEAKER — understands or influences animals and fantastical creatures; one member might calm frightened beasts, another provoke territorial behavior, another direct a trained companion.

THE TINKERER / MACHINE-USER — operates machines, manipulates switches or repairs/dismantles devices; one may be able to hijack specific mechanical defenders with less risk.

THE SORCERER / ENCHANTER — interacts with magical systems, ancient languages or unstable objects. Members vary by spell tradition and acquired ability compatibility.

THE STONE-HEART / HEAVY BODY — resists certain knockback, weights plates, breaks brittle floors or withstands hazards. May overlap with strong characters mechanically; it is okay if one type can substitute for another.

THE SHADOW OR DISGUISE SPECIALIST — can manage suspicion, alter appearance, cloak themselves or redirect attention; may overlap with the tiny infiltrator.

THE WATERWAY SPECIALIST — swims, breathes, moves or manipulates under water; can access hidden flooded structures.

THE RIDER / PILOT — specializes in operating, commandeering or enhancing movement of certain vehicles or mounts; need not be necessary for every vehicle.

These are example capability families, NOT required to be ten classes. Combining or pruning roles may better fit scope.

# Example recruitable individuals and habitats

A burrowing shop scavenger lives in a hidden basement reached by breaking a loose brick; can navigate ventilation and has a special knack for stealing small objects.

A retired arena wrestler hides below the old stands; unusually good at airborne throws and holding powerful foes.

A bird courier lives in an inaccessible skyway post; introduces aerial routes and carries fragile things during flight.

A maintenance apprentice in the waterworks can operate unusual gates and navigate submerged machinery.

A forest creature who speaks with animals may be encountered when the player approaches peacefully; attacking could trigger an entirely different encounter, not necessarily permanently block recruitment.

A famous royal champion might become recruitable after humiliation, rescue, bargain or an extraordinary duel. Exact social conditions open.

A neglected Hall security construct could be repurposed after a dramatic museum incident; also usable as an opposing NPC before recruitment.

A mysterious alchemist's apprentice could make altered-use consumables; recruitment route connects wizard's pills, workshops and world physics.

These are illustrative concepts, not committed characters, names or unlock quests.

# Local recruitment without global roster trivialization

A party may find a resident specialist mid-expedition: a mole-like tunneler, bridge engineer, beast-tamer or courier who can help locally. Perhaps they join as a temporary active character while you are in their home region. Later, a relationship or discovery makes them permanently recruitable.

Exact slot replacement and multiplayer control policy need design. Do not overwrite a human player's active character without consent.

# Functional overlaps make party choice interesting

Imagine the player brings a flyer, strong grappler and creature-speaker. They can reach a high platform, move a gate and speak with forest beasts, but lack a tiny infiltrator to enter a crawlspace. That creates a future revisit—or perhaps the party uses a copied digging power, a movable object or co-op ingenuity to find another route.

The “correct party” should not be one predetermined solution for every location. There should be different viable teams with different discoveries.

# The copied power is a tool, not just a damage type

Candidate power sources:

FIRE — small fire beast, found torch or alchemy. Can blast enemies, ignite flammables, light a path, melt obstacles or cause catastrophes.

ICE — frost creature, enchanted surface or artifact. Can immobilize, freeze moving water or create a temporary support.

WIND — flying foe, weather stone, turbine. Can redirect projectiles, push objects, lift a glider or amplify a jump.

SPARK — mechanical or elemental enemy. Can stun, energize a generator or create a hazard on conductive surfaces.

GRAPPLE / SUPLEX — wrestler enemy, special gauntlet or character move. Can lift/throw, slam against terrain, move blocks or trigger spectacular knockback.

CUTTER / BLADE — tool or enemy attack. Can attack, sever ropes, cut vegetation or disable machinery.

BOMB / EXPLOSION — volatile creature, fuse device or explosive projectile. Can demolish, distract, breach or spectacularly backfire.

SHADOW / INVISIBILITY — enchanted cloak, spectral foe or potion. Supports heists, invisibility, misdirection and escaping heat.

STONE / WEIGHT — armored foe or transformation. Can weigh down a switch, resist force or break cracked flooring.

WHEEL / SPEED — vehicle-like creature or kinetic item. Can launch forward, collide with barriers, traverse tracks or escape patrols.

BEAM / LIGHT — magical device or radiant creature. Can attack, reflect off surfaces or illuminate concealed inscriptions.

ANIMAL CALL — staff, creature pact or charm; can attract or communicate with specific species.

Exact mechanics, source enemies and art are candidates, not finalized power catalog.

# The strongest intersection: type + individual trait + copied power

Example A: a flyer with wind power reaches a very high bell tower, but a tiny character with the same power can send a gust through a ventilation duct to activate a far lever.

Example B: a grappler with invisibility silently lifts a guard into a shadowed alcove; the very same grab can later suplex a heavy armored champion through a weak wall.

Example C: a stone-bodied hero with electricity stands on a pressure plate and conducts power to a machine while another hero drives a stolen vehicle through the opened gate.

Example D: a creature-speaker with fire can negotiate with a dragon, threaten it, ignite its chains or accidentally provoke an overwhelming response.

Example E: a tinkerer with ice can temporarily jam a machine while a teammate takes the contents of its protected chamber.

The point is not a gigantic combination table of scripted solutions; it is a compact set of transferable properties.

# Secret structures across time

A player sees three high windows in the opening castle but cannot yet reach them. Much later they unlock a flyer. The first window connects to the guild rooftops; the second is merely a guard station; the third reveals a rope pulley from which the king's stained-glass throne window can be approached. Different discoveries are useful, dangerous, funny and rewarding in distinct ways.

A small tunnel discovered in the forest leads under a village. Reaching it might require the tiny character, but another player discovers an explosive entrance or water-gate route. Both must remain coherent with physical rules.

A heavily armored machine that defeated the party hours earlier becomes usable after a recruitment or an acquired power changes their approach. The reversal itself can become legendary.

# Character personality as a game invitation

The heroes' shared philosophical indifference is not a script to constantly shout “epic!” Individual curiosities create micro-prompts:

A grappler cannot stop studying the royal champion's armor.

A stealth specialist imagines a perfect treasury raid.

A creature lover hears the captive dragon breathe and wants to meet it.

A tinkerer studies the mechanical restraints and wonders what else they could power.

A flyer eyes a high stained-glass window as a route, not decoration.

These can be conveyed by a glance, idle animation or brief remark, not by floating explanation labels over every object.

# Party management proposals, still open

Player starts with a small subset. Over time, the unlocked roster expands beyond any expedition capacity. Swapping at home/hub or local recruitment sites should feel natural. An optional additional slot could be a reward, but the owner has not chosen party size or whether it expands.

A shared online party needs an intuitive unoccupied-character switch rule and an explicit consent route for exchanging currently controlled characters. Co-op player cap is open.

Acquired powers might be attached to the character or party, but this has NOT been settled. Do not design every area based on one assumptions until tested.

# Art standards for these concepts

Tiny, expressive, readable GBA-era pixel sprites with controlled palettes and consistently scaled motion. The user liked the original Amazing Mirror-like pixel sheets and rejected recent anime-style character illustrations; don't enlarge faces into promotional portraits or clutter the game with details that fight for attention.

# Character prototype success criteria

Recruiting one new character makes a player immediately want to revisit earlier places.

Several characters of the same broad type feel distinct without requiring dozens of proprietary systems.

A temporary copied power feels valuable and changes puzzle/combat/stealth possibilities.

The team can discover at least one valid combination the designer did not explicitly tutorialize.

One limited shared party can handle solo and online co-op without arbitrary human-count requirements.
